This study presents a novel dynamic modeling approach called TD-PAR, a time-varying Poisson autoregressive model with a focus on analyzing and forecasting count-based data over time. The model's structure incorporates both linear and nonlinear regression components to capture complex patterns and trends within such data. To estimate TD-PAR's parameters, an efficient method is introduced that combines a first-order Taylor approximation with an optimization algorithm, specifically the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) method, and further modifies it to account for constrained parameter ranges. The study illustrates the effectiveness of TD-PAR through simulations, demonstrating its ability to accurately estimate parameters and forecast count-based data under various scenarios. Additionally, the model is applied to real-world datasets from sports and economics, showcasing its capability to analyze and predict data in practical settings. The TD-PAR package is available on CRAN for public use.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Numerous molecular dynamics simulations rely on stochastic dynamics algorithms to explore configuration space. As a result of the fluctuation relation, these algorithms guarantee that the system observes a bias in the form of random walk steps that is directly proportional to the force it experiences. With traditional implementations of Langevin dynamics, recovering from this bias requires a time-proportional correction that increases with faster time steps or larger step sizes. Conversely, integrating the noise in stochastic molecular dynamics algorithms eliminates this problem, but it disallows configuration sampling in its classical form. To address this challenge, we develop a new, unbiased stochastic dynamics scheme that directly uses the configuration's Gaussian distribution. We also modify the standard configuration sampling approach to utilize this distribution. By drawing configurations at random from a Gaussian distribution centered on the new position, this method eliminates the need for correcting for the bias in the walk steps. As a result, it produces unbiased simulations that can be concluded with the desired configuration. Furthermore, we include a simple and efficient method for calculating the standard deviation of the distribution. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness on a range of systems, including diatomic molecules, alanine dipeptide, and a small protein, and provide optimized parameters for its use.

Human-generated descriptions of images, typically provided in datasets, serve as a gold standard for assessing the quality of automatic image description systems. We propose a novel evaluation approach that treats these descriptions as labels, much like text data used in language modeling. Our method evaluates an image description model based on its ability to predict the same descriptions, analogous to evaluating a language model on its capacity to predict typical prefixes for existing words. This assessment allows for a more direct analysis of how well an image description model aligns with human preferences, compared to standard evaluation methods that rely on metrics like BLEU and ROGUE. Our results demonstrate that our method yields scores that correlate strongly with human ratings, showcasing its effectiveness in a systematic analysis conducted with six publicly available datasets.

The Euler-Arnold equations originally emerged in the context of classical field theories, particularly in the study of integrable systems, and their solutions give rise to important Lie group identities. We demonstrate that these equations also play a crucial role in classical conformal field theories, specifically in determining the conformal dimension of a generator. This generator, we show, is associated with a particular Lie group, and its conformal dimension can be found by analyzing the equations' solutions, along with the associated Korteweg-de Vries and AKNS equations. We further illustrate our findings with examples from particular Lie groups, including the SL(2) group, and provide a comprehensive discussion on the underlying conditions and methods used.

The forecasts provided in this document are based on the fundamental principles of an extended Skyrme model that incorporates an SU(3) symmetry, in order to predict the properties of possible baryon and meson states. Specifically, we utilize the approach of "soliton formation" to construct adiomic baryons and mesons that fit within the spectrum of 1 to 10 TeV. It is essential to note that these predictions rely on the assumption that certain fundamental representations of the SU(3) symmetry are dynamically broken, which results in the formation of solitons that resemble baryons. To confirm the validity of these predictions, it is crucial to verify that the solitons correspond to the global minimum of the Skyrme model's configuration space. Additionally, we must ensure that the solitons meet the requirements of asymptotic freedom and that their properties align with established knowledge of physics. It is also important to note that certain solitons may not adhere to these conditions, which could render them non-perturbative and thus inaccessible to the extended Skyrme model. A total of 82 possible baryon and meson states are forecasted in this document, along with their predicted properties, including mass ranges, quantum numbers, and two-body decay modes. It is worth mentioning that some of these states might overlap with existing particles or could potentially fit within multiple particle categories. To facilitate further research, a comprehensive table is provided outlining the predicted properties

In our original paper, we exploited the capabilities of SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems to provide additional gains for IEDED transmission. By performing wideband waveforming on data and pilot symbols, we obtained significant improvements in performance. To achieve optimal waveforming strategies, we determined the conditions for the signals' power allocation and derived the maximum achievable gain. Compared to traditional methods utilizing multiple antennas and carriers, our SISO-OFDM waveforming approach yielded a 3dB gain, while the MISO-OFDM variant gained 6dB.

The precision achieved in modern particle physics experiments has created a pressing need for accurate predictions, which are increasingly reliant on detailed information about the structure of quarks and gluons within particles. As a result, there is a growing interest in the precise distribution of quark and gluon flavors within hadrons, exemplified by the "parton distribution functions" (PDFs). Due to the limited information provided by experimental data, there is a recognized need for a comprehensive theoretical framework to guide the fitting process of PDFs. This document aims to provide a detailed overview of the key components, tools, and techniques necessary for constructing such a PDF fitting framework, taking into account both established practices and novel approaches. The document's scope encompasses the fundamental aspects of PDF physics, the relevant theoretical frameworks, the tools and software utilized in PDF analysis, the definition of PDFs, the calculation of cross-sections and observable quantities, the treatment of evolution equations, the implementation of constraints and regularization techniques, the application of Bayesian analysis methods, the generation of Monte Carlo samples, and the validation of fitting procedures.

This study uses a linearized approach to model how a turbulent jet flame reacts to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, and incorporates an active flame model to account for flame oscillations that can create or dampen instability wavelengths within the flame. To accurately represent the interaction between acoustic waves and a jet flame in a linearized system, it is crucial to consider how the flame's oscillations affect the emitted acoustic waves. This is achieved by incorporating an active flame model that takes into account how chemical reactions within the flame influence acoustic wave formation. Utilizing an oven-heated jet arrangement that minimizes initial flow instability, the research team applied a steady laminar flame shape to a turbulent jet flame and examined how acoustic forcing with varying frequencies and amplitudes would impact the flame's behavior. To evaluate the active-flame linearized approach, the team compared it with full RANS and LES simulations of a jet flame under acoustic forcing, and found that it accurately predicted instability wavelength growth in a stable jet flame. However, when a pre-existing instability wavelength is present, the approach may not always replicate simulation results showing wavelength amplification. On the other hand, it did match simulations showing damping of long wavelengths and growth of short wavelengths around an instability peak frequency. To further validate the active-flame linearized approach, it was applied to an unstable jet flame with an initial instability wavelength and compared with large eddy simulation results, which showed that it accurately predicted wavelength evolution under acoustic forcing with varying frequencies.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. This paper explores the connection between the nonlocal integral formulation and the nonlocal differential formulation of the theory, demonstrating that the latter can be derived from the former within a specific framework. Additionally, we examine the fundamental relations of nonlocal gravity, discussing both the constitutive relation and the closure relation, and providing a generalized form that includes a source term. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between the nonlocal differential formulation and the constitutive relation, concluding that both formulations are equivalent when the closure relation is satisfied.

This work examines the potential uses of minor strong interaction symmetry groups, which are proposed as underlying theories beyond the Standard Model, from data taken by the LHC. Since the name "minor system" implies a sub-group of a stronger, potentially un-discovered symmetry, we begin by reviewing research on the TH-U(2)$^3$ model, which some literature refers to as the "minor system". Although it's not commonly classified as a minor system on its own, we also briefly discuss the TH-U(2)$\times$U(2)$^3$ model. We then move on to other proposed minor strong interaction symmetry frameworks, including TH-SO(2)$^3$, TH-Sp(4)/SO(3)$\times$U(1), TH-Sp(4)/GL(3)/ℤ_2, TH-E_6, TH-E_8, TH-F4-$\times$U(1)/ℤ_2, TH-E7(-), TH-E7(+), TH-E8(-), and TH-E8(+), evaluating what particle detection capabilities would be necessary to test them using proton-proton collisions. We also examine the potential approaches for identifying signature patterns of minor strong interaction symmetry groups through experimental research, as well as the proposed search strategies for associated particle composites. Finally, we outline possible research paths for investigating minor strong interaction symmetry groups using future particle detection systems.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries, which exhibit recurring X-ray bursts, have a low incidence rate within the area. This concept is based on an assumption that the recurring pattern of these outbursts is directly linked to the binary system's inclination, which, in turn, is thought to be affected by the binary system's formation preferences. If, however, the underlying pattern is actually related to the binary system's physics, as some studies suggest, then the binary systems' recurrence intervals shouldn't be directly correlated with their inclination. Furthermore, since more wide binary systems are more likely to have lower masses, which also results in lower X-ray outburst peaks, wide neutron star binaries might exhibit longer recurrence intervals. To evaluate the idea that many invisible X-ray binaries contain stellar mass black holes, we examined a sample of 106 known X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's center. We found that, while there is an observed lack of narrow, long recurrence interval neutron star binaries, there is also an increase in the proportion of unidentified X-ray sources among the unobserved binaries with wide orbital periods. This discovery supports the theory that many of these unobserved sources are, in fact, neutron star binaries that are too

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often involves positioning objects from each group in a 2D space. The task of drawing a bipartite graph in an aesthetic format requires determining the optimal placement of its nodes. A widely used method for achieving this is the multilevel layout, which breaks down the graph into smaller subsets and draws each subset at a different distance from the viewer to facilitate an elegant, layered representation. However, calculating the ideal positions for these subsets can be computationally intensive, especially for large graphs. Fortunately, this problem falls into the category of fixed parameter tractability, meaning it can be solved efficiently if a key parameter is known in advance. This parameter, the tree-depth of the graph's clique tree, might seem difficult to determine, but it is actually straightforward to calculate for bipartite graphs. In such cases, the problem is solved in linear time in the size of the graph, making it possible to develop an algorithm that uses the known parameter to solve the problem.

As CPU performance continues to increase, power consumption has surged, leading to a growing need for more efficient processing. This research introduces a novel architecture, HyperDegrade, which significantly reduces the operating frequency of CPUs while minimizing performance degradation. HyperDegrade's two-level hierarchy features a fast low-power core and a slower general-purpose core, which are connected through a novel shared cache. To further optimize performance, a dynamic task partitioning strategy is implemented, which assigns demanding tasks to the general-purpose core and less demanding ones to the fast core. Combining simulation data from cycle-accurate models and real hardware, the research found that HyperDegrade achieves a 74.3% average performance improvement over a conventional high-frequency design, a 3.9 times improvement in energy efficiency, and a 2.4 times reduction in average power consumption for various workloads. Additionally, HyperDegrade delivers a 92% average performance increase and a 3.5 times improvement in energy efficiency compared to a popular low-power CPU.

We introduce a new algorithm called Cross-Over for quickly disentangling a welded circle representing a knot with at most one crossing, simply by reformulating the knot as a polygon and applying a established polygon disentanglement algorithm such as O'Hara's. Compared to other methods, Cross-Over offers significant improvements in our experiments, outperforming the established methods especially for random knots with one crossing.

In a system of multiple robots that perform tasks and share information, cooperation can enhance performance by accomplishing more complex tasks more efficiently. However, the effectiveness of this cooperation depends on the quality of the information exchanged between robots, which is typically limited. In a new approach, we investigate how robots with restricted computing and communication capabilities can organize their information sharing strategy to successfully accomplish tasks that require the comparison of their data. Unlike existing methods that focus on optimizing a single action that yields the best outcome, we seek a strategy that results in all robots performing the same action. To achieve this, we develop an iterative learning process that incorporates the theory of fictitious play and the concept of a "reference point" to help robots approximate the most desirable information sharing approach. We then prove that, under certain conditions, this method guarantees all robots to perform the same action and accomplish the task with the highest difficulty that can be accomplished through information sharing. If no such task exists, the method will converge to a scenario where robots perform the most common action. We also design a simplified alternative approach that eliminates the need for complex calculations between robots.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set and the wreath product of the function group of that set can be effectively represented within the permutation wreath products. Specifically, we established that the representation of the group in question is equivalent to representations of the set's underlying group of symmetry and the derived homomorphism sending that group to the product of its conjugacy classes. Furthermore, we identified specific instances where this representation takes the form of a direct product, specifically for any group that acts simply transitively on a set in a one-to-one correspondence with its points, as well as for any discrete homogeneous ind-discs under the action of the automorphism group.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. In such systems, a randomized access protocol is proposed that takes into account the non-overlapping areas where signals from different antennas are visible to receiving devices. With a vast number of antennas involved, determining the visible areas is complex, leading to a need for a precise analysis of visible region intersections. However, intriguingly, research shows that the distribution of non-overlapping visible area boundaries is identical to the distribution of overall visible area boundaries. Therefore, the author is able to utilize previously established findings regarding the distribution of visible area boundaries to calculate the average number of bits required for region identification, helping to design an optimization strategy for signal power levels.

Neural text generation models have excelled in predicting words based on context, but their performance can be outshined by traditional n-gram models when evaluating small changes in texts like word order. To improve neural models and leverage the advantage of n-gram models, we propose a novel architecture that learns from the gap between contextual information and n-gram models. In a supervised learning setting, our model demonstrates comparable performance to neural models when there's ample training data and significantly outperforms them when data is scarce. Furthermore, our model requires significantly less parameters than neural models, indicating a strong ability to learn from the n-gram model residuals with minimal additional learning.

The security concerns surrounding traditional Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems have prompted the development of an enhanced variant, Informed OCR, which incorporates additional information such as the expected outcomes and casting instructions to improve the accuracy of ballot tabulation. As the use of ballot marking devices (BMDs) increasingly generates ballots with printed text, there's a growing need to address the poor BMD-generated text recognition rates. In this research, we introduce an innovative Informed OCR approach, leveraging the casting instructions and expected outcomes to compensate for BMD-generated text difficulties. Furthermore, we propose a novel method to utilize the casting instructions for BMD-generated text recognition, taking into account the varying font sizes and styles. Experimental results indicate that Informed OCR significantly outperforms traditional OCR systems, with our approach achieving the highest accuracy of 95.4% compared to 84.5% for the standard OCR, following the established evaluation criteria.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

This study formulates the reciprocal gamma function in terms of an integral that can be evaluated using a specific Hankel path, illustrating the function's relationship with the ordinary gamma function. We then introduce a weighted version of the function, incorporating a positive weight function, and show that this variant is analogous to the original, allowing its representation as an evaluable integral.

We have adapted the conventional hydrodynamic theory to accommodate the demands of simulating nonequilibrium dynamics for interacting Bose gases within a quantum framework. This modified approach emphasizes the utilization of phase-space Fock representations to effectively manage the evolution of both wave functions and their corresponding densities, ensuring that the theory remains fully quantum-compliant. Notably, this adaptation bypasses the necessity of solving complex second-order partial differential equations while also addressing issues related to quantum noise and condensate fragmentation. By incorporating the Fock representation into the theory, we have created a framework that is exceptionally suited for employing numerical methods like phase-space hybrid classical-quantum (hcq) simulations to explore the dynamics of these systems. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we have performed a series of hcqNLESDI simulations for a collapsing Bose--Hubbard condensate on an optical lattice, investigating the emergence of quantum noise and fragmentation while also verifying the convergence of the results in relation to the employed Fock representation sizes.

Deep Neural Networks have achieved immense success in various tasks, thanks to their ability to learn from massive data sets. However, their high dimensional parameter space and the need for large data sets to train them pose significant challenges. One promising approach to overcoming these challenges is the Instructor-Student architecture, where a student network learns from the weights of an already trained instructor network. This method has shown considerable potential in both knowledge distillation and knowledge learning for teacher-student networks. Despite the growing interest in this architecture, recent advances in teacher-student networks are not well organized in the literature, necessitating a comprehensive survey to explore the various Instructor-Student architectures, their theoretical foundations, and their applications. This survey delves into the theoretical aspects of Instructor-Student architectures, examines the various knowledge learning methods, discusses promising research directions, and provides a thorough analysis of the theoretical results. With its in-depth examination of the Instructor-Student architecture's capabilities and limitations, this survey serves as an ideal starting point for future research endeavors.

We introduce a new efficient algorithm that uses a brief function representation, combining a linear base function and a low-degree polynomial correction, to quickly solve exactly the Most Probable Explanation and constrained optimisation problems within graphical models. This new method surpasses existing methods by utilizing the same model parameters and structure, and is particularly effective when dealing with models featuring log-linear parameters and structures that are low-degree or have a simple base function. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new approach is particularly suitable for models with simple base functions and low-degree polynomial corrections, and can be employed to solve larger-scale models more efficiently.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant of this algebra, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through its universal envelope, denoted as $U(Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2))$. The centralizer $C_{\mathfrak{h}}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, or the centralizer of the simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ within its own Lie algebra, is then utilized to derive the defining relations of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. The centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is further connected to the centralizer $C_{\mathfrak{h}}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ to establish a Hilbert-Poincar\'e series for the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. The resulting formula is then utilized to calculate the dimension of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through its irreducible representation of highest weight $\lambda$. The approach is then generalized

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of existing work means that implementing a paired-permutation test correctly is often challenging. To address this, an alternative method using precise paired-permutation tests has been proposed, utilizing structured test statistics. The proposed approach is more efficient than the traditional method, reducing the computational burden significantly. In addition, precise paired-permutation tests allow for the use of faster approximation methods for initial tests, further minimizing the workload. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the new approach, an experimental protocol was implemented, consisting of three key experiments. The results show that the precise paired-permutation test yields more precise results compared to the traditional method, requiring significantly less time and effort in the process.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

This study develops a Poisson single-sensor Poisson Bold Multi-Bernoulli (PMBB) filter that utilizes a partially grid-based origin model. Unlike traditional methods that use a single point origin, this approach accounts for possible deviations from the expected origin when calculating the mean and covariance of the distribution. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the partially grid-based origin model by applying the Poisson single-sensor PMBB filter to a scenario where multiple sensors share the same origin, and an unknown origin is assumed to be within a defined grid. The results show that the filter can accurately estimate the number and positions of targets, as well as the presence or absence of clutter, even when some sensors are malfunctioning or have uncertain origins. The most effective sensor configuration is also determined, which involves optimizing the placement and field of view of the sensors to provide the best possible detection and tracking of targets.

In the realm of soccer games, determining the most effective action to take in critical moments on the field is a complex task that requires quick decision-making. This challenge is particularly pronounced for automated agents seeking to succeed in such situations, which are influenced by numerous factors including the game's state, player positions, and time remaining. To address this challenge, a system was developed utilizing a deep reinforcement learning algorithm that integrates a long short-term memory network to enable automated agents to execute the most advantageous actions in critical game situations, surpassing human-controlled agents in simulated matches. The proposed methodology was tested in a simulator and demonstrated significant improvements in scoring goals and avoiding goals, thereby establishing a foundation for applying deep reinforcement learning in the control of automated soccer players.

The development of local dynamic vortex (LDV) signal processing techniques has enabled the use of single-point LDV systems to obtain two-dimensional vortex wake structure measurements behind cylinders or airfoils without the need for multiple LDV systems. By applying a phase-locking average (PLE) technique to time-varying signal data from a single point, two-dimensional vortex wake structure measurements can be obtained. This method eliminates the expense of multiple LDV systems while providing the necessary data to calculate three-dimensional vortex wake structure models.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in the Klein-Gordon equation linked to an anharmonic oscillator. A key aspect of our approach is the transformation that recasts the equation in a Hamiltonian form, emphasizing the role of the anharmonic oscillator's parameters. Utilizing this formulation, we establish criteria for the stability of solitary waves based on the equation's spectrum and the anharmonic oscillator's behavior. In particular, we identify a critical parameter range where the solitary wave solutions become unstable. Moreover, we outline a straightforward method for determining the exact instability growth rates when solitary waves lose stability.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral, light particles that interact weakly would greatly benefit from a deeper understanding of the system. Specifically, it's challenging to determine whether these particles might be undetectable or if they decay before interacting with other particles. A new approach has been proposed to address this issue, utilizing data from experiments like the Belle II facility that involves searching for missing energy. This method relies on analyzing decay patterns of certain particles, such as $B$ mesons, which can take various forms and behave differently when interacting with these weakly interacting particles. By applying advanced statistical techniques to analyze the data, researchers can better comprehend the properties of these particles and their possible masses, as well as the sensitivity of future experiments like Belle II. This understanding is crucial for developing effective research strategies for identifying these particles.

The rise of contextualized language models has revolutionized text processing, leading to exceptional performance in various tasks. Recently, these models have been successful in detecting semantic changes between texts. In this work, we explore the potential of these models to identify altered sentences while also learning the underlying reasons for these changes. To accomplish this, we trained multiple contextualized language models on a specific domain (law) and evaluated their ability to capture semantic differences. We utilized a dataset consisting of pairs of original and altered sentences, drawn from either a large existing corpus or a smaller established dataset. The results, obtained using three distinct models (RoBERTa, BART, and SPIDEr), showed that they all performed remarkably well in identifying altered language. Notably, we observed significant variations in performance when analyzing different types of semantic changes. To further our understanding, we examined the underlying mechanisms by analyzing the attention distributions within the models. We found that contextualized language models tend to focus on words directly related to the alteration, demonstrating their ability to grasp the context. Additionally, we classified the semantic changes into multiple categories, allowing for a deeper understanding of the kinds of alterations the models could identify. Ultimately, our research provides insights into the capabilities and limitations of contextualized language models for detecting and analyzing semantic changes in language.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses a large sample of AGN, consisting of radio-quite and radio-bright jets, to determine the spin of heavy black holes via the observation of infrared emission and the phenomenon of superradiance. The data indicates that heavy black holes with low jet powers and those in radio-quiet jets exhibit significant alignment between their jets' orientation and the surrounding environmental magnetic fields. Additionally, a notable increase in the fraction of black holes with extreme spin is observed at high redshifts. The findings support a model linking black hole spin, through the mechanism of superradiance, with the formation of aligned jets and, in a larger sense, the environment surrounding black holes. The results also provide crucial constraints on the possible masses of ultralight axions and similar particles, with a limit of 10^-20 erg set at the E=1$\mu$eV energy level for a wide range of particle wavelengths, independent of black hole mass.

The paper applies Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods to solve the time-dependent equation for a driven quantum harmonic oscillator. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on steady-state conditions, this method captures both short and long-time behavior of the system by representing the quantum state as a discrete grid of values. A key innovation is the derivation of an unbiased estimate for the transition kernel, exploited to obtain accurate representations of the Wigner function and expectation values of key operators. To further enhance the method's utility, it is implemented using Path Integral Monte Carlo, which allows for the inclusion of reservoir effects in optomechanical systems by treating the oscillator's environment as a driven harmonic oscillator. The results obtained using this approach for a single-photon driven optomechanical system demonstrate its effectiveness in both transient and steady-state scenarios, navigating complex parameter spaces and illustrating the formation of quantum nonlinearities. The code used is publicly available, offering a foundation for future applications in more complex systems and configurations.

We have developed a quantitative Hoare logic for quantitative relational properties, suitable for programs with interactions. Unlike existing methods, this system addresses the challenge of defining a tripartite preconditions that account for both initial relational properties and future expectations. We have established a soundness proof for our approach and demonstrated its effectiveness by applying it to a variety of case studies, including examples with unbounded memory and those involving conditional updates of relational states.

The National Solar Observatory (NSO) vector magnetic field data is widely utilized for predicting properties of the sun's behavior, including solar flares and eruptions. However, recent controversies surrounding the data's reliability have raised concerns about its accuracy, particularly for areas near the solar equator. A 2020 data gap, resulting from allegations of espionage linked to a building rental issue, further complicated the situation. To address the accuracy issues and data gap, a comprehensive error analysis was conducted for vector magnetic field measurements derived from spectrographs. Noise and bias sources were identified, and a new correction method was developed, incorporating an estimation of noise levels. The revised analysis revealed that the data's errors were significantly underestimated previously, and many affected regions could be rescued from the error-prone data set with the updated measurements. Ultimately, a temporary data set was created to bridge the 2020 gap, ensuring the continuity of solar flare risk assessment research.

This work establishes that the group of square-free classes modulo an odd prime $p$ forms a Boolean group under the operation of composition of cyclotomic classes, in addition to being a distributive lattice under the meet operation. A detailed description of this structure is provided, utilizing the fact that the lattice is distributive, which is then used to prove that every subgroup of the multiplicative group of a finite field $GF(n)$ that is normalized by the $p$-Sylow subgroup of the group of $n$-th residues is congruent to a subgroup of the group of $n$-th residues under the discrete logarithm.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in a space with a time component, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in cases where a specific distance measurement doesn't vary.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of interpersonal if-then relationships, comprising approximately 560k unique statements. Each statement is categorized into one of 278 possible events, which are further grouped into 23 overall events. We have also developed a method for classifying these statements into cause, effect, or both. Evaluating cause and effect requires an in-depth understanding of context, as seen in examples like "If I'm hungry, then I need food." We have performed various analyses and established a clear pathway for future research.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of new view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing methods that only consider a single view, our network processes both near and far near-view images to generate a new view. This approach utilizes a dual representation, combining local and global features that allows our model to learn from both viewpoints and adapt to any desired view. By leveraging both near and far near-view images, our approach can predict videos from extremely far-away views that current state-of-the-art methods struggle with. In our experiments with realistic datasets, our method significantly outperformed the competition when predicting views with large angles, demonstrating remarkable performance with an average PSNR of 40.2 and average SSIM of 0.83 when predicting views 75 degrees away from the near-view.

The dimension of a metric space is a crucial concept that originated in geometry, emphasizing the minimal number of points needed to determine the distance between any two locations within the space by using their relative distances. A famous result by Gerstenhaber and Weil states that the dimension of a metric space is at most two if its unit distance sets form a vector space over the reals, which implies that areas are one-dimensional. In the context of graphs, the concept of dimension has various definitions, with the cubic distance dimension being the most well-known, requiring the least number of points to determine distances. We introduce the "trimmed" dimension, excluding very small distances, which is particularly significant for graphs with large distances varying little. Building upon this, we establish an upper bound for the cubic distance dimension of a graph based on its trimmed dimension, which is an important achievement. We also investigate specific graph types, determining their trimmed and cubic distance dimensions to be 2-dimensional, unless they are interval graphs, which in that case, the dimension is 1-dimensional.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study proposes a new method that combines cardiac auscultation sounds with recorded background noises and maps these composite sounds into high-dimensional spaces using convolutional neural networks (CNNs).  After training on large datasets of recorded sounds, the study finds that the proposed method outperforms current techniques by up to 30% in noise-free conditions and shows promising results when tested with clinically recorded sounds from multiple countries.  To further evaluate the method's potential for use in low-resource settings, the authors conduct additional experiments in Ethiopia and the Philippines, where it achieves high accuracy even with low-cost recording devices.  As a result, the study suggests using CNNs to transform cardiac auscultation sounds into more recognizable patterns and integrates the method with current techniques for improving condition detection.

Observations of galactic molecular gas reservoirs are often analyzed using dust temperature maps, which may not accurately represent the conditions of interest when studying specific lines like CI. Since dust temperatures are typically derived from lines like CO(1-0), which may not be in equilibrium with CI, there could be significant deviations, particularly in cases of strong far-IR sources or dusty outflows. To address this issue, we examine the relationship between dust temperatures and the excitation temperatures of CI(1-2) and CI(2-3), which are directly related to the line ratios but are independent of dust models. By doing so, we create a more reliable estimate for the gas temperature, which is crucial for many applications, including the calculation of molecular gas masses and the study of gas dynamics. Notably, we find that CI lines are more effective than CO lines in tracing the gas temperature, especially in extremely dusty regions. This finding suggests that observing the CI lines could be particularly valuable for studying the temperature structure of molecular gas, especially in galaxies with active star formation or those with strong outflows, and may also be useful for analyzing the gas conditions in systems with unusually high dust temperatures or low CO emission, such as some lensing systems and ultra-luminous infrared galaxies.

We establish that in ASEP, a system where particles represent vehicles on a road or individuals in a population, a Markov process can be defined and analyzed to predict the short-term evolution of particle velocities. This process is analogous to the AWKM model, which applies to ASEP but with particles representing positions rather than vehicles. The generator of the AWKM model is known, allowing us to determine the transition probabilities for the ASEP velocity process in the next step, which we calculate to be uniform across possible configurations. Additionally, we derive the equilibrium measure of the ASEP velocity process, which is found to be a product measure of the equilibrium measure of ASEP and a Bernoulli distribution with a parameter representing the particle density.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues that have arisen between public health officials, policymakers, data scientists, and mathematicians. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic spread, and critical time periods for data. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from biology, economics, and sociology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the practical implications of mathematical models may result in difficulties implementing effective policies to combat the pandemic, highlighting the necessity for cross-disciplinary understanding and collaboration.

The connection between the mass of galaxies and the rate at which they form stars remains a topic of substantial interest and debate. Previous research has established a positive, nonlinear link between these two factors, with more massive galaxies generally exhibiting lower star formation rates, despite possessing the necessary gas to produce more stars. Several factors, including environmental, structural, and physical properties of galaxies, have been examined for their potential role in shaping this relationship. At the center of massive galaxies, a black hole can exert influence on the star formation process through its radiative output, and in more extreme cases, through its active state. To investigate the role of black hole radiation and nuclear activity in forming and altering the shape of the mass-star formation rate connection, a comprehensive analysis was conducted. This study combined the largest sample of local galaxies to date, consisting of 8000 star-forming galaxies observed by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, with the most detailed and up-to-date inventory of black hole masses. The results reveal that the radio jet activity of a galaxy's nucleus has a significant impact on its position within the mass-star formation rate relationship, with jets helping to suppress star formation around mid-sized massive galaxies but exhibiting no notable effect on the smallest or largest galaxies in the sample. The findings suggest that the nonlinear shape of the mass-star formation rate connection is primarily influenced by the balance between black hole jet power and the mass of the galaxy, with a threshold of power required for jets to significantly impact star formation.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of tweets based on both the tweet's language and the
interaction between languages. We develop a multi-task learning approach to
accomplish this task, combining tasks from diverse language settings to
enhance the performance of a single model. We introduce an all-purpose
sentiment dictionary to aid in learning valuable emotional information and
design a novel attention mechanism to facilitate the model's language
awareness. We conduct experiments using English, Spanish, and French data,
demonstrating significant improvements in performance compared to single-
task learning. The developed approach achieves the best results when the
languages share similar grammatical structures, indicating a strong link
between language setup and performance.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a mysterious process occurring within a less massive and less rapidly rotating star that has contracted to a smaller size at its surface. By analyzing data from the Kepler space telescope over the course of 4 years, we observed an increase in the star's rate of rotation and a decrease in its surface temperature, accompanied by oscillatory behavior. To understand this behavior, we considered various theoretical models, including those that account for the merger with a smaller, more rapidly rotating star in an earlier phase of the star's evolution, as well as models that allow for the transfer of angular momentum between layers within the star. Based on our analysis, we cannot determine whether this event occurred as a result of a star merging with a smaller companion that has since disappeared, or if it resulted from the distribution of angular momentum within the star following a significant loss of mass. To confirm our findings, observations are necessary to determine the star's actual radius and mass, as well as the masses of any potential companion stars.

False news spreads rapidly on social media platforms due to the immediacy of information shared there. Although false news often gets corrected over time, its initial dissemination can cause significant consequences. The rapid spread of false information poses a significant threat to individuals, communities, and societies. With the increasing volume of information shared online, automated systems to detect false news are more essential than ever. In situations where false news emerges suddenly, there is a particular need for a system that can quickly identify it. This research proposes an automated method to detect emerging false news on social media using a combination of neural network architectures and little available data. This method consists of two stages: the first stage involves training a neural network to learn the common features between true and false news, and the second stage involves training another neural network to pinpoint the distinct characteristics of false news. This approach takes advantage of meta-learning techniques to quickly adapt to new, previously unseen false news. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, experiments were conducted using real-world data from FactCheckWars and Snopes. The results showed that the system outperformed existing methods in detecting emerging false news on social media.

Recently, Golay complementary arrays have gained popularity due to their ability to generate sets of signals with unique autocorrelation and cross-correlation properties. This paper introduces designs for multi-component Golay complementary arrays and presents a method for constructing pairs of higher-order Golay complementary arrays. Specifically, we have developed formulas for constructing pairs of fourth-order and eighth-order GCA arrays and designed sets of GCA arrays with different components to serve various applications. Additionally, we explored the concept of nearly GCA arrays and identified sets of signals that nearly comply with GCA arrays' definitions. All designed arrays are available for immediate use in research.

A method for generating simulated brain injury data using a combination of a Generative Adversarial Network and a Variational Auto-Encoder has been proposed. The proposal utilizes a single view of 3D MRI scans and demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating a label embedding technique to address overfitting when using categorical data. The model's ability to capture important features and reduce noise in raw data has been confirmed through analysis. To prove the utility of the proposed approach for brain injury simulation, experiments were conducted using both single-task and multi-task learning setups and compared to an existing method. The results show that the proposed approach generates more accurate synthetic data and leads to better performance when training models on simulated data.

A new unified architecture is proposed for feature learning through contrastive learning, combining both local and global contrast minimization objectives. The design incorporates two learning tasks: a global contrast task that matches similar samples and a local contrast task that compares samples from the same class. The architecture's effectiveness is demonstrated by embedding both tasks within a single neural network, allowing for the sharing of feature maps and reducing the model's parameter size. The framework's capabilities are illustrated through its application in both single-view and multi-view settings, showcasing its ability to learn effective features and achieve high performance in various scenarios without the need for explicit label information.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the complexity of these models and the vast amount of data they process pose significant challenges in updating their knowledge, particularly with respect to structured information like databases, wikis, and knowledge graphs. In this work, we introduce a method to efficiently inject structured knowledge into LLMs by using a small existing knowledge-base of ours as a template for training the model on structured data. We demonstrate that our approach yields LLMs with high accuracy on queries drawn from a large knowledge-graph, outperforming existing methods on multiple evaluation metrics. We also conduct experiments showing the effectiveness of our technique in updating knowledge on existing models without degradation, reducing the need for costly training from scratch.

In this research, we examine how the angular dependence of a black hole's shadow can provide valuable information about its rotation parameter, specifically when observing from a location with a simple geometry, such as a planar or hyperbolic space. We begin by reviewing the reefing phenomenon, where a slot forms in the shadow due to the focusing of light near the event horizon, and how this phenomenon is influenced by the black hole's spin. Then, we explore how the reefing pattern changes for a rotating, charged AdS black hole, analyzing how its shadow's shape and size are affected by both its spin and charge, as well as the observer's inclination. To accomplish this analysis, we use both the near-horizon geometry of the black hole and the Reissner-Nordstr\"om metric, employing the conserved quantity's slope to calculate the temperature of the gas near the bifurcation point on the timelike geodesic. A code was also developed to plot the shadow's shape from different viewing angles, which shows that the shadow's size and shape are inversely proportional to the distance between the observer and the black hole. Furthermore, we derive an equation that relates the shadow's largest deformation angle to the black hole's spin and charge, allowing for the possible separation of these two parameters even when they are close in value.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, and measuring certain aspects of the state can be particularly challenging. The phase-sensitive quadrature amplitudes, for example, are difficult to measure directly, which motivates the use of non-local measurements like homodyne or heterodyne detection that can, in principle, determine these values. However, since these methods rely on the phase of the light used in the measurement, their accuracy is limited by phase fluctuations, which are a hallmark of complex systems like lasers. A better approach might involve using the Wigner function, which provides a complete picture of the state by encoding both local and non-local properties of the system. The Wigner function allows us to study the relationship between different phase-sensitive quadrature amplitudes and their fluctuations, which is crucial for understanding how quantum systems behave and interact. Specifically, it can help us comprehend the conditions under which systems like optical lattices or superconducting circuits transition from a state of free evolution to one of synchronized oscillations, as well as the generation of entanglement between separate components of the system. In such situations, analyzing the Wigner function or the related tomogram of the state might offer valuable insights, which we intend to explore in the following work by examining how its features change in response to variations in certain parameters or conditions.

Using a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb, we investigate the decay modes $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$. We determine the branching fractions for these decays to be $2.8 \times 10^{-4}$, $1.5^{+0.7}_{-0.5}\times 10^{-4}$ for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{D}^0$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{D}^0$*(2600), $1.5^{+0.7}_{-0.5}\times 10^{-4}$ for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^* \bar{D}^0$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{D}^*$(2600), and $2.4^{+1.4}_{-1.1}\times 10^{-5}$ for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^* \bar{D}^*$(2600) after combining

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a complicated task. Despite the method developed by Stanley to build such lattices from their join and meet lattices, we face the challenge of pinpointing the join and meet lattices of a module's submodules lattice when dealing with modules such as $k[G/N]$ for a group $G$ and its subgroup $N$. In this research, we devise an approach to construct the lattice of submodules of $k[G/N]$ by gathering information about the lattices of submodules of its submodules, specifically those corresponding to the subgroups of $N$. This process begins with the submodules associated with the subgroups of $N$ that are minimal with respect to a given condition, which in this case is being maximal with respect to being disjoint from $N$. We then apply a recursive construction to include other subgroups of $N$, drawing on the relationship between subgroups and submodules as well as the structure of their lattices. This method yields a combinatorial model for the lattice of submodules of $k[G/N]$ as an interval lattice within the product lattice of the lattices of submodules of its submodules corresponding to the subgroups of $N$, allowing for a straightforward description of its structure.

We explore the connections between certain geometric conditions and specific curvature properties that a submanifold might exhibit when immersed within the Euclidean space. Specifically, we examine the relationship between being a Biharmonic submanifold and being subject to recurrent dynamics, as well as the relationship between the harmonic and biharmonic operators in the context of the de Rham differential operator's spectral decomposition. Our investigation involves analyzing how these connections are affected by different geometric configurations, including spheres, hyperbolic spaces, and their products, and we outline a straightforward method for computing the biharmonic operator's spectrum in the case of spheres.

Consider a probability distribution defined by a rational number p/q. We are giving a concise definition for p/q-identifiable sets, which consists of points whose coordinates correspond to outcomes of a random experiment following this probability distribution. Specifically, we are providing a description of sets defined by (p-q)/q-identifiable points as unions of identifiable sets defined by points with integer coordinates, and as a result, we are giving a proof that such sets are always identifiable in the (p-q)/q-scale.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to derive key parameters for both models.

A highly persistent myth exists that random acoustic signals emitted by cracking adhesive tapes signify true randomness. We dispute this claim by demonstrating that these signals, despite appearing disordered, contain embedded patterns and structures. Using a set of materials with varying properties and through both theoretical and experimental approaches, we uncover the underlying mechanisms generating these patterns. We find that within certain frequency ranges, the patterns correlate with shear modulus values of the materials, showcasing an unambiguous connection between structural properties and acoustic signal patterns. To further explore these findings, we develop a simple model simulating the creation of these patterns, which reveals that they result from the interaction between stress waves and the growing crack. This research challenges the notion that random processes always generate truly random outcomes and highlights the importance of analyzing noise signals in a physical context.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. This abstract definition incorporates the idea of measuring distances between points in a way that is consistent and symmetric. It also introduces the notion of an angle between two curves, defined as the infimum of the values that represent the maximum possible combination of distances between points on those curves. Menger presented two problems concerning the representation of angles in a way similar to real numbers, and the embedding of angle spaces into a more general structure that would allow for such a representation. Initially, these problems were discussed in the context of metric spaces, but Menger also considered the application of these ideas to semi-metric spaces. We address these problems by demonstrating that any semi-metric space can be embedded into a real vector space in a way that is consistent with the angle function. This achievement builds upon previous work by G. Navara, in which he showed that any semi-metric space can be represented within a Banach space. Our method of proof exploits the fact that the space of real homogeneous polynomials is isomorphic to a Banach space under the sup norm. This is a key factor in utilizing the Navara representation to obtain a continuous embedding that preserves the angle function. This achievement marks the initial step in developing a theory of angle functions within the realm of semi-metric spaces, paving the way for further research.

Our proposed TPC model is a convolutional neural network designed to predict 3D shapes from sparse depth images, achieving the best performance to date on the established PointCloud From Depth dataset, thereby establishing a new benchmark. Our approach deviates from traditional methods that utilize local point transformations to enhance sparse depth maps, instead employing a technique that generates unique transformation profiles to counter local pattern duplication. To train our model effectively, we introduce a novel regularization strategy that accounts for overlapping kernel areas, reducing the need for extensive point cloud data. Our code is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/ghourian/PointCloud-From-Depth.

Consider a program taking input from a vector space and producing output in a vector space, with programs and inputs/output spaces all defined through abstract geometric concepts rather than specific vectors. Without loss of generality, we can assume the input and output spaces are subspaces of a larger vector space known as the "model space". Under these conditions, testing the program involves determining whether it distorts or preserves the geometric structures within the input/output spaces. If the program maintains the geometric structure, it meets the requirements; if it alters the structure in a predictable way, such as mirroring shapes, the testing process can also be defined as it aligns with the structure preservation principle. Notably, reflective programs that flip the geometric structure are particularly simple to test as they only require testing on half of the input space due to their symmetry.
We provide a detailed explanation for a proposed algorithm in [_KLNL] that uses Kummer theory to determine the clear Serre weights for GL_2. This algorithm is an alternative to the one found in [DN].

Advanced composite materials with self-sensing capabilities are being developed for potential use in critical structural applications. As a result, researchers are exploring methods to intentionally damage these structures in a precise and controlled manner. This study proposes a novel concept called "exact damage shaping" where electrical impedance tomography is utilized in conjunction with genetic algorithms to deliberately create complex damage patterns within self-sensing composite materials. A key aspect of this research is the development of an optimization strategy to distribute multiple electrical excitation points effectively, ensuring high-quality image reconstruction and accurate damage mapping. A computer model was employed to design and test this method, demonstrating its effectiveness by successfully shaping various damage configurations in a single composite lamina. The results show that this technique can create a wide range of damage patterns, even mimicking damage that extends across multiple laminae. As a result, exact damage shaping presents a promising approach for various applications, including the development of smart structures capable of withstanding and adapting to complex stress profiles.

In Euclidean geometry, we can identify lines and circles with points, allowing us to define dimensions of a geometric space in a way that is independent of the traditional dimension numbering system. This approach enables the use of geometric constructions to define numbers, as seen in constructive mathematics, and facilitates the development of geometric vector spaces that are suitable for physics. We can define a vector space over a geometric integral domain in a way that mirrors the traditional approach, using components and scalar multiplication, while also introducing the concepts of module homomorphisms and tensor products in a physics context. Specifically, we can define tensor products in a way that is consistent with the integral domain definition, allowing physicists to work with tensor products over geometric vector spaces, even in situations involving negative dimensions, modular lattices, and fractal geometry.

A right-angled Artin group can be viewed as a fundamental group of a graph's complement, and its associated variety is reflected in its abstract structure. We establish that for a right-angled Artin group, the abstract embedding into a product group is mirrored by a geometric embedding of its associated graph into a product graph, whose components are simply connected. This topological splitting is useful in understanding the underlying graph's structure, particularly when analyzing the graph's components that are not simply connected, as it allows us to utilize tools developed for simply connected graphs.

The development of GPU-accelerated algorithms for fast iterative matrix inversion has gained significant traction, prompting our response. Building upon our previous work, we have enhanced our approach to tackle issues related to current algorithms, specifically the lack of higher order techniques and the ineffectiveness of previous implementations on GPUs. The updated methods we present, second-order and third-order recursive iterative algorithms, have been put through their paces on a variety of systems, demonstrating notable performance gains over the original first-order technique when utilizing massive machine learning architectures, while also exhibiting substantial performance improvements when executed on conventional CPUs.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound as if contexts were fully observable. This achievement is notable as it outperforms existing bounds by a significant margin. This achievement particularly occurred when the time horizon is substantial. When the distribution is known the approach offers an information theoretically optimal bound of order O(\sqrt{TC}\log(T)). A simple and effective learning algorithm is also put forward. This algorithm uses a learning approach that is context-oblivious and utilizes approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the distribution is unknown. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems, potentially generating turbulence and affecting the development of planetary formation through the sedimentation of particles like dust. While VSI can generate turbulence to counteract the settling of dust particles, an excess of dust may actually stabilize the VSI, leading to a decrease in turbulence and an increase in dust settlement. To better understand the interactions between VSI, dust settlement, and turbulence, a comprehensive study was conducted, focusing on the VSI's onset and growth rates in the upper regions of the disk system and analyzing the underlying physical mechanisms. The research revealed that VSI is more difficult to initiate and stabilize in areas with higher dust particle sizes, which settle more quickly towards the disk's bottom. Additionally, an increase in dust particle sizes reduces the extent of the VSI's activity. As particles settle, VSI's influence decreases, creating a positive feedback loop that accelerates the settlement of larger dust particles and may even prevent the VSI from developing in many areas of the disk system. The findings suggest that VSI is not a primary source of turbulence in the outer regions of the disk system, especially in areas with large dust particles, and other instability factors, such as the global VSI or local instabilities like the non-linear g-mode instability, may take its place.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in deep learning techniques have been compromised by ingenious design flaws called artificial design flaws or intentional source code errors known as backdoors. Unlike traditional attacks that aim to deceive models by exploiting vulnerabilities, backdoors are purposefully embedded in models to perform specific actions when certain conditions are met, such as recognizing particular sounds or images. Generally, research on backdoors has focused on computer vision models, specifically CNN-based models, and has been explored in areas like image classification and generation. To investigate the possibility of incorporating backdoors in models, various methods have been deliberately introduced and analyzed by researchers. Notably, a technique called Global Mean Pooling Backdoor (GMB) has been found to effectively insert backdoors in models without noticeably affecting their performance on clean data, according to a study published in 2022. Contrary to other backdoor methods that rely on additional triggers, the GMB technique utilizes existing image features, making it particularly hard to detect. To further explore the GMB method, an original architecture called Dynamic Global Mean Pooling (DGMB) was developed, which integrates the standard Global Mean Pooling layer in deep neural networks. Surprisingly, it was discovered that even without pre-training the model on contaminated data, a backdoor could be successfully implanted in a model by simply pre-training it on a dataset that had been artificially corrupted with a specific pattern.
